topics.title: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary
topics.summary: Definitions in this glossary follow the usage of this volume. Product-specific guarantees must still be checked against the selected implementation and version. Similar names do not make two mechanisms interchangeable.

blocks.text: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary
rich: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Definitions in this glossary follow the usage of this volume. Product-specific guarantees must still be checked against the selected implementation and version. Similar names do not make two mechanisms interchangeable.
rich: Definitions in this glossary follow the usage of this volume. Product-specific guarantees must still be checked against the selected implementation and version. Similar names do not make two mechanisms interchangeable.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Acceptance. The service’s defined commitment to handle work. In HarborDispatch, acceptance means a matching gateway row has committed; it does not mean the worker has completed.
rich: The service’s defined commitment to handle work. In HarborDispatch, acceptance means a matching gateway row has committed; it does not mean the worker has completed.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Acknowledgement. A message reporting a particular stage of handling. Its meaning depends on the protocol: receipt, broker persistence, consumer handling, and business-effect commitment are different acknowledgement boundaries.
rich: A message reporting a particular stage of handling. Its meaning depends on the protocol: receipt, broker persistence, consumer handling, and business-effect commitment are different acknowledgement boundaries.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Admission control. A decision about whether new work becomes the system’s responsibility, based on policy and available resources. Rejection should remain distinct from failure after durable acceptance.
rich: A decision about whether new work becomes the system’s responsibility, based on policy and available resources. Rejection should remain distinct from failure after durable acceptance.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Applied revision. The position through which committed changes have been incorporated into a replica’s serving state. Receiving or persisting a log entry does not necessarily mean queries already reflect it.
rich: The position through which committed changes have been incorporated into a replica’s serving state. Receiving or persisting a log entry does not necessarily mean queries already reflect it.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Artifact identity. A stable reference to a specific built output, commonly associated with a checksum and provenance. A branch name alone can change and is not a complete artifact identity.
rich: A stable reference to a specific built output, commonly associated with a checksum and provenance. A branch name alone can change and is not a complete artifact identity.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Asynchronous completion. A result delivered after the initiating call has returned or suspended. Correct handling requires ownership of operation state and a rule for cancellation, stale generations, and cleanup.
rich: A result delivered after the initiating call has returned or suspended. Correct handling requires ownership of operation state and a rule for cancellation, stale generations, and cleanup.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Atomicity. The property that a defined group of state changes is committed together or not committed under the resource’s transaction model. It does not automatically include unrelated external effects.
rich: The property that a defined group of state changes is committed together or not committed under the resource’s transaction model. It does not automatically include unrelated external effects.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Authority. The component or protocol entitled to decide a particular state transition. Architecture should identify authority for uniqueness, receipts, membership, credentials, and migration rather than assuming it from network location.
rich: The component or protocol entitled to decide a particular state transition. Architecture should identify authority for uniqueness, receipts, membership, credentials, and migration rather than assuming it from network location.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Backoff. A delay policy between attempts, often increasing after repeated failure. Backoff reduces some retry pressure but does not by itself bound fleet-wide concurrency or make unsafe retries idempotent.
rich: A delay policy between attempts, often increasing after repeated failure. Backoff reduces some retry pressure but does not by itself bound fleet-wide concurrency or make unsafe retries idempotent.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Backpressure. A mechanism that limits upstream production according to downstream capacity. It needs an explicit propagation and overload policy rather than merely moving work into another unbounded queue.
rich: A mechanism that limits upstream production according to downstream capacity. It needs an explicit propagation and overload policy rather than merely moving work into another unbounded queue.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Binary compatibility. Compatibility among compiled components at their ABI boundary. Source compatibility, Pimpl, and matching function names do not automatically guarantee compatible object layout, runtimes, or allocation ownership.
rich: Compatibility among compiled components at their ABI boundary. Source compatibility, Pimpl, and matching function names do not automatically guarantee compatible object layout, runtimes, or allocation ownership.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Bulkhead. A resource partition that limits how one work class can exhaust capacity needed by another. Its protection depends on shared resources below the partition as well as visible thread pools.
rich: A resource partition that limits how one work class can exhaust capacity needed by another. Its protection depends on shared resources below the partition as well as visible thread pools.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Cache floor. In the teaching model, the minimum acceptable version retained after invalidation. It prevents a late older fill from repopulating the cache after the old value was removed.
rich: In the teaching model, the minimum acceptable version retained after invalidation. It prevents a late older fill from repopulating the cache after the old value was removed.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Canonical request. A representation of the fields that determine an operation’s meaning after validation and normalization. Duplicate recognition compares canonical meaning rather than incidental textual formatting.
rich: A representation of the fields that determine an operation’s meaning after validation and normalization. Duplicate recognition compares canonical meaning rather than incidental textual formatting.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Checkpoint. A recorded recovery position or state. Its semantics must specify which work is complete; advancing past unfinished work can lose processing even when later work has finished.
rich: A recorded recovery position or state. Its semantics must specify which work is complete; advancing past unfinished work can lose processing even when later work has finished.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Circuit breaker. A stateful admission policy for a dependency, often using closed, open, and half-open states. It limits repeated failing calls but does not repair the dependency or undo remote effects.
rich: A stateful admission policy for a dependency, often using closed, open, and half-open states. It limits repeated failing calls but does not repair the dependency or undo remote effects.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Commit point. The point at which a resource reports that a transaction or state transition is committed under its guarantees. Client observation of that commit is a separate event.
rich: The point at which a resource reports that a transaction or state transition is committed under its guarantees. Client observation of that commit is a separate event.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Compensation. A new business action intended to address a previous partial effect. It may not restore the exact prior world and requires its own identity, failure handling, and verification.
rich: A new business action intended to address a previous partial effect. It may not restore the exact prior world and requires its own identity, failure handling, and verification.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Consensus. Agreement on decisions under a defined distributed failure model. Broadcasting messages or assigning a leader number does not implement the complete protocol and its safety and progress conditions.
rich: Agreement on decisions under a defined distributed failure model. Broadcasting messages or assigning a leader number does not implement the complete protocol and its safety and progress conditions.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Consistency model. The contract governing which observations and orderings clients may see. It should be expressed through operation histories, not only vague terms such as strong or current.
rich: The contract governing which observations and orderings clients may see. It should be expressed through operation histories, not only vague terms such as strong or current.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Consumer offset. A position in a particular log partition or stream. It is a transport coordinate and should not automatically replace a domain event identifier that must survive export or replay.
rich: A position in a particular log partition or stream. It is a transport coordinate and should not automatically replace a domain event identifier that must survive export or replay.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Correlation identifier. Metadata connecting observations related to work. A job key, attempt ID, and trace ID can be correlated while retaining different scopes and lifetimes.
rich: Metadata connecting observations related to work. A job key, attempt ID, and trace ID can be correlated while retaining different scopes and lifetimes.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Deadline. The latest eligible completion or waiting boundary under a defined clock and policy. A caller’s expired wait does not prove that a remote mutation did not commit.
rich: The latest eligible completion or waiting boundary under a defined clock and policy. A caller’s expired wait does not prove that a remote mutation did not commit.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Dead-letter handling. A controlled path for work that cannot complete under ordinary retry policy. It needs ownership, retention, diagnosis, and authorized redrive rather than becoming an ignored backlog.
rich: A controlled path for work that cannot complete under ordinary retry policy. It needs ownership, retention, diagnosis, and authorized redrive rather than becoming an ignored backlog.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Deduplication receipt. Retained information binding an operation identity to its accepted meaning and effect. Its retention and atomic relationship to the effect determine the scope of duplicate safety.
rich: Retained information binding an operation identity to its accepted meaning and effect. Its retention and atomic relationship to the effect determine the scope of duplicate safety.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Degradation. A deliberate reduction in supported capability, such as rejecting new mutations while serving status. It should remain explicit and observable rather than being disguised as ordinary success.
rich: A deliberate reduction in supported capability, such as rejecting new mutations while serving status. It should remain explicit and observable rather than being disguised as ordinary success.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Delivery attempt. One transport or execution try for a logical operation. Several attempts can correspond to one retained business effect when the idempotency contract is preserved.
rich: One transport or execution try for a logical operation. Several attempts can correspond to one retained business effect when the idempotency contract is preserved.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Deterministic model. A controlled representation whose inputs, event order, and time can be reproduced. It supports reasoning about selected histories but does not automatically model all real-world failures.
rich: A controlled representation whose inputs, event order, and time can be reproduced. It supports reasoning about selected histories but does not automatically model all real-world failures.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Discovery revision. An ordering token for membership information within a defined authority domain. Restarting or replacing that authority requires an explicit generation or continuity policy.
rich: An ordering token for membership information within a defined authority domain. Restarting or replacing that authority requires an explicit generation or continuity policy.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Drain. A lifecycle phase that stops new admission while settling already admitted work under a bounded policy. Resource destruction should follow completion or cancellation ownership, not precede it.
rich: A lifecycle phase that stops new admission while settling already admitted work under a bounded policy. Resource destruction should follow completion or cancellation ownership, not precede it.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Durable intent. Persisted state representing an accepted obligation that can be resumed after process loss. In this book, pending gateway rows serve this role and drive later delivery.
rich: Persisted state representing an accepted obligation that can be resumed after process loss. In this book, pending gateway rows serve this role and drive later delivery.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Effect boundary. The resource or protocol within which a business change is considered committed. A local database transaction cannot automatically include an email provider or another independent service.
rich: The resource or protocol within which a business change is considered committed. A local database transaction cannot automatically include an email provider or another independent service.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Epoch. A generation identifying an authority or state-machine interval. It lets a component reject stale completions or stale ownership, provided generation issuance and comparison are defined correctly.
rich: A generation identifying an authority or state-machine interval. It lets a component reject stale completions or stale ownership, provided generation issuance and comparison are defined correctly.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Error budget. The allowed amount of bad service outcomes under a specified objective, denominator, and window. It is a policy tool, not a substitute for correctness invariants.
rich: The allowed amount of bad service outcomes under a specified objective, denominator, and window. It is a policy tool, not a substitute for correctness invariants.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Event identity. A stable identifier for a domain occurrence. It should remain associated with the same meaning across redelivery and may need to survive changes in transport position.
rich: A stable identifier for a domain occurrence. It should remain associated with the same meaning across redelivery and may need to survive changes in transport position.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Eventual consistency. A convergence-oriented contract under stated conditions. The label alone does not define intermediate reads, conflict resolution, uniqueness, or the treatment of externally visible promises.
rich: A convergence-oriented contract under stated conditions. The label alone does not define intermediate reads, conflict resolution, uniqueness, or the treatment of externally visible promises.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Executor. An abstraction controlling where and when work runs. A coroutine does not automatically provide an executor, and serialized execution does not necessarily imply one fixed operating-system thread.
rich: An abstraction controlling where and when work runs. A coroutine does not automatically provide an executor, and serialized execution does not necessarily imply one fixed operating-system thread.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Fencing token. An ordered ownership generation checked by the protected resource to reject stale writers. It requires a trustworthy issuer and preserved state; a client-chosen integer is not authority.
rich: An ordered ownership generation checked by the protected resource to reject stale writers. It requires a trustworthy issuer and preserved state; a client-chosen integer is not authority.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Framing. The protocol mechanism that identifies message boundaries in a byte stream. TCP’s stream behavior does not preserve the boundaries of individual application writes.
rich: The protocol mechanism that identifies message boundaries in a byte stream. TCP’s stream behavior does not preserve the boundaries of individual application writes.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Generation check. A comparison ensuring that an asynchronous result still belongs to the state that may accept it. The result can remain informationally useful even when its state-update authority is stale.
rich: A comparison ensuring that an asynchronous result still belongs to the state that may accept it. The result can remain informationally useful even when its state-update authority is stale.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Graceful shutdown. A controlled transition that stops admission, settles or cancels work under policy, joins execution, and releases resources. It still needs a bounded fallback for uncooperative work.
rich: A controlled transition that stops admission, settles or cancels work under policy, joins execution, and releases resources. It still needs a bounded fallback for uncooperative work.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Idempotency. A contract under which repeated attempts at the same defined operation do not create additional unintended effects. Identity scope, payload association, retention, and atomicity determine its actual guarantee.
rich: A contract under which repeated attempts at the same defined operation do not create additional unintended effects. Identity scope, payload association, retention, and atomicity determine its actual guarantee.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Inbox. Consumer-side retained state used to recognize already handled messages or operations. For crash-safe effect deduplication, its receipt must be atomic with the relevant local effect.
rich: Consumer-side retained state used to recognize already handled messages or operations. For crash-safe effect deduplication, its receipt must be atomic with the relevant local effect.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Invariant. A property that must remain true across every supported state transition, including failure and recovery. Examples include stable key meaning and rejection of stale ownership generations.
rich: A property that must remain true across every supported state transition, including failure and recovery. Examples include stable key meaning and rejection of stale ownership generations.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Jitter. Random variation applied to timing, often retry delays, to reduce synchronization among callers. It does not replace a rate, concurrency, or total resource budget.
rich: Random variation applied to timing, often retry delays, to reduce synchronization among callers. It does not replace a rate, concurrency, or total resource budget.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Lease. Time-bounded authority under a coordinator’s rules. Lease expiration can permit reassignment but does not forcibly stop an old process or revoke every delayed external write.
rich: Time-bounded authority under a coordinator’s rules. Lease expiration can permit reassignment but does not forcibly stop an old process or revoke every delayed external write.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Linearizability. A consistency contract in which each operation appears to take effect between invocation and completion while respecting real-time precedence. It is more specific than generic data validity.
rich: A consistency contract in which each operation appears to take effect between invocation and completion while respecting real-time precedence. It is more specific than generic data validity.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Logical clock. An ordering mechanism based on events and communication rather than elapsed physical time. Increasing logical values do not by themselves prove causality between unrelated events.
rich: An ordering mechanism based on events and communication rather than elapsed physical time. Increasing logical values do not by themselves prove causality between unrelated events.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Membership. The set of participants considered eligible under a service or coordination protocol. A local list is not automatically an authoritative or current view of the cluster.
rich: The set of participants considered eligible under a service or coordination protocol. A local list is not automatically an authoritative or current view of the cluster.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Monotonic read. A session property preventing observations from moving backward through already observed versions under the service’s defined conditions. Routing affinity alone may not preserve it after failure.
rich: A session property preventing observations from moving backward through already observed versions under the service’s defined conditions. Routing affinity alone may not preserve it after failure.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Outbox. Producer-side durable state tying business intent to an outgoing delivery obligation. A dispatcher can replay it after failure, while the receiver still needs appropriate duplicate handling.
rich: Producer-side durable state tying business intent to an outgoing delivery obligation. A dispatcher can replay it after failure, while the receiver still needs appropriate duplicate handling.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Partial failure. A condition in which some components or communication paths fail while others continue. It creates uncertainty that cannot be modeled as one process returning a single error code.
rich: A condition in which some components or communication paths fail while others continue. It creates uncertainty that cannot be modeled as one process returning a single error code.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Partition key. The value used to choose a data or work authority. It should align with the invariants and ordering scope that must remain local or coordinated.
rich: The value used to choose a data or work authority. It should align with the invariants and ordering scope that must remain local or coordinated.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Poison message. Work that repeatedly fails for a persistent reason rather than a transient outage. It requires explicit terminal handling or repair to avoid indefinite retries and starvation.
rich: Work that repeatedly fails for a persistent reason rather than a transient outage. It requires explicit terminal handling or repair to avoid indefinite retries and starvation.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Principal. A representation of verified identity and relevant claims used for authorization. Untrusted payload fields must not become a principal merely because they use familiar names.
rich: A representation of verified identity and relevant claims used for authorization. Untrusted payload fields must not become a principal merely because they use familiar names.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Provenance. Evidence describing how an artifact was produced, including relevant inputs and build process. A checksum establishes byte identity only relative to a trusted expected value.
rich: Evidence describing how an artifact was produced, including relevant inputs and build process. A checksum establishes byte identity only relative to a trusted expected value.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Quorum. A set of participants whose agreement satisfies a protocol’s rule. Intersection arithmetic is necessary for some designs but does not replace voting, persistence, log, or membership-transition rules.
rich: A set of participants whose agreement satisfies a protocol’s rule. Intersection arithmetic is necessary for some designs but does not replace voting, persistence, log, or membership-transition rules.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Readiness. Eligibility to receive a defined class of work. It differs from liveness and may change during dependency degradation, initialization, draining, or capacity exhaustion.
rich: Eligibility to receive a defined class of work. It differs from liveness and may change during dependency degradation, initialization, draining, or capacity exhaustion.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Reconciliation. A controlled comparison and repair process among authoritative states after uncertainty or divergence. It should preserve evidence and authorization rather than silently overwrite conflicting meaning.
rich: A controlled comparison and repair process among authoritative states after uncertainty or divergence. It should preserve evidence and authorization rather than silently overwrite conflicting meaning.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Redrive. An authorized attempt to resume previously failed or quarantined work. It should preserve the original logical identity when recovering the same effect and record the reason and actor.
rich: An authorized attempt to resume previously failed or quarantined work. It should preserve the original logical identity when recovering the same effect and record the reason and actor.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Rendezvous placement. A selection method that scores key-candidate pairs and chooses a deterministic winner. Stable mapping properties do not copy state or authorize a new owner during migration.
rich: A selection method that scores key-candidate pairs and chooses a deterministic winner. Stable mapping properties do not copy state or authorize a new owner during migration.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Replay. Reprocessing retained work or events from a defined point. Pure projection rebuilds and external side effects require different policies so recovery does not accidentally repeat business actions.
rich: Reprocessing retained work or events from a defined point. Pure projection rebuilds and external side effects require different policies so recovery does not accidentally repeat business actions.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Retry budget. A bound on attempts, elapsed time, rate, or another resource for recovery work. Multiple nested retry owners can multiply load beyond each layer’s apparent local limit.
rich: A bound on attempts, elapsed time, rate, or another resource for recovery work. Multiple nested retry owners can multiply load beyond each layer’s apparent local limit.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Saga. A workflow that represents partial progress and coordinates recovery or compensation across independent effects. It is not a universal atomic transaction or automatic reversal of the world.
rich: A workflow that represents partial progress and coordinates recovery or compensation across independent effects. It is not a universal atomic transaction or automatic reversal of the world.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Schema compatibility. The ability of specified readers and writers to interpret stored or transmitted data with preserved meaning. Successful parsing is necessary but not sufficient when units or semantics change.
rich: The ability of specified readers and writers to interpret stored or transmitted data with preserved meaning. Successful parsing is necessary but not sufficient when units or semantics change.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Service-level indicator. A measured definition of service behavior with a specified numerator, denominator, and boundary. Submission acceptance and accepted-job completion are different indicators in this volume.
rich: A measured definition of service behavior with a specified numerator, denominator, and boundary. Submission acceptance and accepted-job completion are different indicators in this volume.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Snapshot. A representation of state at a defined point. Recovery may require a matching log position, schema, receipt history, and authority generation; copying visible rows alone can be incomplete.
rich: A representation of state at a defined point. Recovery may require a matching log position, schema, receipt history, and authority generation; copying visible rows alone can be incomplete.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Strand. In asynchronous execution terminology, a mechanism for serializing associated handlers. It does not automatically imply a dedicated thread or solve object lifetime outside its execution contract.
rich: In asynchronous execution terminology, a mechanism for serializing associated handlers. It does not automatically imply a dedicated thread or solve object lifetime outside its execution contract.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Tail latency. Behavior in the slow portion of a latency distribution. A good average can coexist with unacceptable long waits, especially under queueing, contention, or periodic recovery work.
rich: Behavior in the slow portion of a latency distribution. A good average can coexist with unacceptable long waits, especially under queueing, contention, or periodic recovery work.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Token bucket. A rate-admission model with bounded burst capacity and replenishment. It controls a different resource dimension from simultaneous concurrency and queued memory.
rich: A rate-admission model with bounded burst capacity and replenishment. It controls a different resource dimension from simultaneous concurrency and queued memory.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Trace context. Metadata used to connect spans across boundaries under a tracing standard. It is not a credential and should not grant authorization merely because a caller supplies it.
rich: Metadata used to connect spans across boundaries under a tracing standard. It is not a credential and should not grant authorization merely because a caller supplies it.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Unknown outcome. A result in which the caller cannot determine whether a remote effect committed. Stable identity, status lookup, and reconciliation can manage it without inventing a new operation.
rich: A result in which the caller cannot determine whether a remote effect committed. Stable identity, status lookup, and reconciliation can manage it without inventing a new operation.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

blocks.text: Write-ahead log. A storage mechanism recording changes before they are incorporated into other serving structures. Its durability, checkpoint, backup, and recovery semantics depend on the implementation and configuration.
rich: A storage mechanism recording changes before they are incorporated into other serving structures. Its durability, checkpoint, backup, and recovery semantics depend on the implementation and configuration.
blocks.headingContext: Appendix F — Architecture and Distributed-Systems Glossary

Acceptance. The service’s defined commitment to handle work. In HarborDispatch, acceptance means a matching gateway row has committed; it does not mean the worker has completed.

Acknowledgement. A message reporting a particular stage of handling. Its meaning depends on the protocol: receipt, broker persistence, consumer handling, and business-effect commitment are different acknowledgement boundaries.

Admission control. A decision about whether new work becomes the system’s responsibility, based on policy and available resources. Rejection should remain distinct from failure after durable acceptance.

Applied revision. The position through which committed changes have been incorporated into a replica’s serving state. Receiving or persisting a log entry does not necessarily mean queries already reflect it.
Artifact identity. A stable reference to a specific built output, commonly associated with a checksum and provenance. A branch name alone can change and is not a complete artifact identity.

Asynchronous completion. A result delivered after the initiating call has returned or suspended. Correct handling requires ownership of operation state and a rule for cancellation, stale generations, and cleanup.

Atomicity. The property that a defined group of state changes is committed together or not committed under the resource’s transaction model. It does not automatically include unrelated external effects.

Authority. The component or protocol entitled to decide a particular state transition. Architecture should identify authority for uniqueness, receipts, membership, credentials, and migration rather than assuming it from network location.

Backoff. A delay policy between attempts, often increasing after repeated failure. Backoff reduces some retry pressure but does not by itself bound fleet-wide concurrency or make unsafe retries idempotent.

Backpressure. A mechanism that limits upstream production according to downstream capacity. It needs an explicit propagation and overload policy rather than merely moving work into another unbounded queue.

Binary compatibility. Compatibility among compiled components at their ABI boundary. Source compatibility, Pimpl, and matching function names do not automatically guarantee compatible object layout, runtimes, or allocation ownership.
Bulkhead. A resource partition that limits how one work class can exhaust capacity needed by another. Its protection depends on shared resources below the partition as well as visible thread pools.
Cache floor. In the teaching model, the minimum acceptable version retained after invalidation. It prevents a late older fill from repopulating the cache after the old value was removed.

Canonical request. A representation of the fields that determine an operation’s meaning after validation and normalization. Duplicate recognition compares canonical meaning rather than incidental textual formatting.
Checkpoint. A recorded recovery position or state. Its semantics must specify which work is complete; advancing past unfinished work can lose processing even when later work has finished.

Circuit breaker. A stateful admission policy for a dependency, often using closed, open, and half-open states. It limits repeated failing calls but does not repair the dependency or undo remote effects.
Commit point. The point at which a resource reports that a transaction or state transition is committed under its guarantees. Client observation of that commit is a separate event.
Compensation. A new business action intended to address a previous partial effect. It may not restore the exact prior world and requires its own identity, failure handling, and verification.

Consensus. Agreement on decisions under a defined distributed failure model. Broadcasting messages or assigning a leader number does not implement the complete protocol and its safety and progress conditions.
Consistency model. The contract governing which observations and orderings clients may see. It should be expressed through operation histories, not only vague terms such as strong or current.
Consumer offset. A position in a particular log partition or stream. It is a transport coordinate and should not automatically replace a domain event identifier that must survive export or replay.
Correlation identifier. Metadata connecting observations related to work. A job key, attempt ID, and trace ID can be correlated while retaining different scopes and lifetimes.
Deadline. The latest eligible completion or waiting boundary under a defined clock and policy. A caller’s expired wait does not prove that a remote mutation did not commit.

Dead-letter handling. A controlled path for work that cannot complete under ordinary retry policy. It needs ownership, retention, diagnosis, and authorized redrive rather than becoming an ignored backlog.

Deduplication receipt. Retained information binding an operation identity to its accepted meaning and effect. Its retention and atomic relationship to the effect determine the scope of duplicate safety.

Degradation. A deliberate reduction in supported capability, such as rejecting new mutations while serving status. It should remain explicit and observable rather than being disguised as ordinary success.
Delivery attempt. One transport or execution try for a logical operation. Several attempts can correspond to one retained business effect when the idempotency contract is preserved.

Deterministic model. A controlled representation whose inputs, event order, and time can be reproduced. It supports reasoning about selected histories but does not automatically model all real-world failures.
Discovery revision. An ordering token for membership information within a defined authority domain. Restarting or replacing that authority requires an explicit generation or continuity policy.
Drain. A lifecycle phase that stops new admission while settling already admitted work under a bounded policy. Resource destruction should follow completion or cancellation ownership, not precede it.
Durable intent. Persisted state representing an accepted obligation that can be resumed after process loss. In this book, pending gateway rows serve this role and drive later delivery.

Effect boundary. The resource or protocol within which a business change is considered committed. A local database transaction cannot automatically include an email provider or another independent service.

Epoch. A generation identifying an authority or state-machine interval. It lets a component reject stale completions or stale ownership, provided generation issuance and comparison are defined correctly.
Error budget. The allowed amount of bad service outcomes under a specified objective, denominator, and window. It is a policy tool, not a substitute for correctness invariants.
Event identity. A stable identifier for a domain occurrence. It should remain associated with the same meaning across redelivery and may need to survive changes in transport position.

Eventual consistency. A convergence-oriented contract under stated conditions. The label alone does not define intermediate reads, conflict resolution, uniqueness, or the treatment of externally visible promises.

Executor. An abstraction controlling where and when work runs. A coroutine does not automatically provide an executor, and serialized execution does not necessarily imply one fixed operating-system thread.

Fencing token. An ordered ownership generation checked by the protected resource to reject stale writers. It requires a trustworthy issuer and preserved state; a client-chosen integer is not authority.
Framing. The protocol mechanism that identifies message boundaries in a byte stream. TCP’s stream behavior does not preserve the boundaries of individual application writes.

Generation check. A comparison ensuring that an asynchronous result still belongs to the state that may accept it. The result can remain informationally useful even when its state-update authority is stale.

Graceful shutdown. A controlled transition that stops admission, settles or cancels work under policy, joins execution, and releases resources. It still needs a bounded fallback for uncooperative work.

Idempotency. A contract under which repeated attempts at the same defined operation do not create additional unintended effects. Identity scope, payload association, retention, and atomicity determine its actual guarantee.
Inbox. Consumer-side retained state used to recognize already handled messages or operations. For crash-safe effect deduplication, its receipt must be atomic with the relevant local effect.
Invariant. A property that must remain true across every supported state transition, including failure and recovery. Examples include stable key meaning and rejection of stale ownership generations.
Jitter. Random variation applied to timing, often retry delays, to reduce synchronization among callers. It does not replace a rate, concurrency, or total resource budget.
Lease. Time-bounded authority under a coordinator’s rules. Lease expiration can permit reassignment but does not forcibly stop an old process or revoke every delayed external write.

Linearizability. A consistency contract in which each operation appears to take effect between invocation and completion while respecting real-time precedence. It is more specific than generic data validity.
Logical clock. An ordering mechanism based on events and communication rather than elapsed physical time. Increasing logical values do not by themselves prove causality between unrelated events.
Membership. The set of participants considered eligible under a service or coordination protocol. A local list is not automatically an authoritative or current view of the cluster.

Monotonic read. A session property preventing observations from moving backward through already observed versions under the service’s defined conditions. Routing affinity alone may not preserve it after failure.
Outbox. Producer-side durable state tying business intent to an outgoing delivery obligation. A dispatcher can replay it after failure, while the receiver still needs appropriate duplicate handling.
Partial failure. A condition in which some components or communication paths fail while others continue. It creates uncertainty that cannot be modeled as one process returning a single error code.
Partition key. The value used to choose a data or work authority. It should align with the invariants and ordering scope that must remain local or coordinated.
Poison message. Work that repeatedly fails for a persistent reason rather than a transient outage. It requires explicit terminal handling or repair to avoid indefinite retries and starvation.
Principal. A representation of verified identity and relevant claims used for authorization. Untrusted payload fields must not become a principal merely because they use familiar names.
Provenance. Evidence describing how an artifact was produced, including relevant inputs and build process. A checksum establishes byte identity only relative to a trusted expected value.

Quorum. A set of participants whose agreement satisfies a protocol’s rule. Intersection arithmetic is necessary for some designs but does not replace voting, persistence, log, or membership-transition rules.
Readiness. Eligibility to receive a defined class of work. It differs from liveness and may change during dependency degradation, initialization, draining, or capacity exhaustion.

Reconciliation. A controlled comparison and repair process among authoritative states after uncertainty or divergence. It should preserve evidence and authorization rather than silently overwrite conflicting meaning.
Redrive. An authorized attempt to resume previously failed or quarantined work. It should preserve the original logical identity when recovering the same effect and record the reason and actor.
Rendezvous placement. A selection method that scores key-candidate pairs and chooses a deterministic winner. Stable mapping properties do not copy state or authorize a new owner during migration.

Replay. Reprocessing retained work or events from a defined point. Pure projection rebuilds and external side effects require different policies so recovery does not accidentally repeat business actions.
Retry budget. A bound on attempts, elapsed time, rate, or another resource for recovery work. Multiple nested retry owners can multiply load beyond each layer’s apparent local limit.
Saga. A workflow that represents partial progress and coordinates recovery or compensation across independent effects. It is not a universal atomic transaction or automatic reversal of the world.

Schema compatibility. The ability of specified readers and writers to interpret stored or transmitted data with preserved meaning. Successful parsing is necessary but not sufficient when units or semantics change.

Service-level indicator. A measured definition of service behavior with a specified numerator, denominator, and boundary. Submission acceptance and accepted-job completion are different indicators in this volume.
Snapshot. A representation of state at a defined point. Recovery may require a matching log position, schema, receipt history, and authority generation; copying visible rows alone can be incomplete.

Strand. In asynchronous execution terminology, a mechanism for serializing associated handlers. It does not automatically imply a dedicated thread or solve object lifetime outside its execution contract.
Tail latency. Behavior in the slow portion of a latency distribution. A good average can coexist with unacceptable long waits, especially under queueing, contention, or periodic recovery work.
Token bucket. A rate-admission model with bounded burst capacity and replenishment. It controls a different resource dimension from simultaneous concurrency and queued memory.
Trace context. Metadata used to connect spans across boundaries under a tracing standard. It is not a credential and should not grant authorization merely because a caller supplies it.
Unknown outcome. A result in which the caller cannot determine whether a remote effect committed. Stable identity, status lookup, and reconciliation can manage it without inventing a new operation.

Write-ahead log. A storage mechanism recording changes before they are incorporated into other serving structures. Its durability, checkpoint, backup, and recovery semantics depend on the implementation and configuration.
